query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, spray‐coated layer of 2D high‐entropy alloy nanoflakes, applied on the CoCrFeNi matrix surface, will enable in situ formation of a robust, lubricious tribofilm during sliding that reduces both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) compared to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its native microstructure (unmodified surface, as typically prepared for sliding tests) used as the baseline.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin coating via air spray deposition of 2D HEA nanoflakes (e.g. a composition such as (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 that has demonstrated tribo-catalytic activity) onto the surface of the CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.conditions: Sliding (dry friction) tests conducted under variable loads and sliding speeds in ambient atmosphere over the temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C. The test parameters (normal load, sliding speed, and sliding distance) remain the same for both coated and uncoated samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in situ tribofilm – primarily an amorphous lubricious layer generated by the tribocatalytic activity of the 2D HEA nanoflakes – that protects the base alloy and reduces direct metal–metal contact.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the stress and friction at the interface activate the nanoplatelets, which catalyze the dissociation or rearrangement of available surface species (and, in some cases, trace environmental carbon sources), promoting the formation of a self-sustaining low-shear tribofilm. This film minimizes adhesive interactions and plastic deformation of the underlying alloy over a wide range of operating temperatures, including the challenging high-temperature regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated CoCrFeNi sample will exhibit a lower average coefficient of friction and a reduced specific wear rate relative to the uncoated baseline; while the exact magnitude is uncertain, the improvement should be qualitatively observable across tests from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The uncoated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy tested under identical sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 800 °C; load and sliding speed as controlled variables in dry sliding tests under ambient conditions.
generation.uncertainty: It is not yet fully established whether the 2D HEA nanoflake-induced tribofilm will remain stable and active at the highest temperature (≈800 °C), so performance in that regime might show some variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy specimens: one set with a spray-coated layer of 2D HEA nanoflakes and one set without any coating. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding tests under a range of temperatures from room temperature up to 800 °C, using the same load and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Continuous recording of the friction coefficient during sliding tests.
Post-test measurement of wear track volume (e.g., via 3D optical interferometry) to calculate specific wear rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in both average friction coefficient and specific wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the uncoated specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

Intrigued by the extensive lubricious behavior of the HEA in ethanol, a further study has been conducted to analyze the capabilities of HEA nanoflakes in other solvents like water. The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the starting COF decreases with an increase in load, showing the intrinsic HEA behavior like in the case of HEA in ethanol. However, the HEA in water exhibits limited wear resistance and high wear rates in the magnitude of 10−6 mm3 (N∙m)−1 as compared to HEA in ethanol which has wear rates in the magnitude of 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1. This shows that the ethanol solvent plays a significant role in increasing the tribological performance of HEA during friction tests.
